overview.body:
**Amaterasu** ​(*amaterasu*) — ‌Sun ‌Goddess, Shintō ​· ​Sun goddess ​in ​Shinto — ​belongs ‌to the ​Japanese ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Sun Goddess, ​Shintō". ​The name ​means ​"Sun goddess ​in ‌Shinto"[^1].

**Amaterasu** ​is ‌the central ​deity ‌of the ​Japanese ‌pantheon, the ​sun ‌itself made ​divine ​and the ‌ancestral kami ‌of ‌the imperial ​house. ​Her realm ‌is ​Takamagahara, the ​High ‌Plain of ​Heaven. ​Without her ‌light, ​rice cannot ‌grow, ​order collapses, ​and ​the world ​sinks ‌into darkness.[^2]

‌PuniCodex ​restores the ‌name ​as **Amaterasu** ​and serves ‌its ‌temple at ‌[its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/amaterasu/). The ​restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent form ​— ​a description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed ​form itself. ​The ‌plain ASCII ​form ​*amaterasu* survives ​as ‌a modern ​convenience ‌imposed by ​the early ‌domain-name ​system; the ‌restoration, ‌not the ​fallback, ​is the ​form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki 1–2 (variant births, Yamato-hime and the founding of Ise).

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Japanese characters ​as ​**天照**. ​Etymologically it ​means ‌"Sun ​goddess in ​Shinto"[^1].

‌The ​ASCII form ‌*amaterasu* ​survives ‌only because ​the ​early domain-name ​system ​could ​not carry ‌diacritics; ​it ‌is a ​technological ‌compromise, ​not an ‌ancient ​spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration ​**Amaterasu** ‌recovers the ‌full ‌diacritic detail ​of ​the ‌scholarly transliteration ​directly ​in ‌the address ​bar. ​The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ‌— ​a description ​computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form ‌itself.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- **a** ​→ ‌**A** ‌— Same
- ‌**m** ‌→ ​**m** — ‌Same
- ​**a** ​→ **a** ​— ‌Same
- ​**t** → ​**t** ​— ‌Same
- **e** ​→ ​**e** — ​Same
- ‌**r** ​→ **r** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**a** → ​**a** ‌— ‌Same
- **s** ​→ ​**s** ​— Same
- ​**u** ‌→ ‌**u** — ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/a.ma.te.ɾa.sɯ/** — ​Modern ​Standard Japanese ​(Hepburn).[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ‌**Ama-** — ​Open ​front [a], ‌labiodental [m], ​open central ‌[a]; from ​天 ‌'heaven/sky'
- **-tera-** ​— Alveolar ​tap [ɾ] ​between close-mid ​[e] ​and open ‌central [a]; ​from 照 ‌'to ​shine'
- **-su** ‌— Voiceless ​alveolar fricative ‌[s] plus ​close ‌back unrounded ​[ɯ]; the ​final vowel ‌is soft

‌For ‌the modern ​speaker, the ​closest approximation ‌is: 'ah-mah-TEH-rah-soo' ​— ​the 'r' ‌is a ​light tap, ​and the ‌final ​'u' is ‌barely voiced.

​Kindred and ​historical forms ​of ​the name:

- ‌**Japanese** — ‌天照 (Amaterasu), ​short for ‌Amaterasu-ōmikami, ​'Heaven-Illuminating Great ​August Deity' ‌— 天 ‌is the ‌very ‌character for ​sky
- **Siblings** ‌— Tsukuyomi ​(moon) and ​Susanoo ​(storms), born ‌with her ​in Izanagi's ​misogi
- ​**Lineage** — ‌Grandmother of ​Ninigi; divine ​ancestress of ​the ‌imperial line ​through Jimmu

‌Amaterasu is ​a plain ‌restoration ​here: the ‌ASCII form ‌is identical ​to Hepburn ​romanization. ​Her authority ​is mythological ‌and political, ‌not phonetically ​distinctive.

domains.body:
**Amaterasu** ​is ‌the central ‌deity ​of ​the ​Japanese ​pantheon, the ​sun ‌itself ​made ​divine and ‌the ​ancestral ‌kami ​of the ‌imperial ​house. ​Her ​realm ​is Takamagahara, ​the ‌High ​Plain ‌of Heaven. ​Without ‌her ​light, ‌rice ​cannot grow, ‌order ​collapses, ​and ‌the world ‌sinks ‌into ​darkness.[^1]

### ​Sun Sovereign

‌Ruler ​of ​Takamagahara; ‌her ​light ripens ​the ‌rice ​and ‌orders the ​day.

### ​Imperial ​Ancestor

​Grandmother ‌of Ninigi, ‌whose ​line ‌produced ​Jimmu, first ​emperor ‌of ‌Japan.

### ‌Weaver and ‌Cultivator

​She ‌presides ​over ​the heavenly ​weaving ‌hall; ​Susanoo's ​outrage there ​triggered ‌the ​cave ​crisis.

### ​Withdrawal and ‌Return

​Her ‌seclusion ​in Ama-no-Iwato ‌and ​the ‌ruse ‌of the ​mirror ​remain ​the ​pattern ‌of every ‌restored ​order.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki 1–2 (variant births, Yamato-hime and the founding of Ise).

symbols.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with ‌Amaterasu concentrates ​in ​a small ​set ​of recurring ​attributes, each ‌a ​compressed statement ​about ‌the name:[^1]

- ​**Mirror ‌(yata no ​kagami)** ‌— One ​of ​the Three ​Imperial ​Regalia; the ​mirror ‌hung outside ​the cave ‌showed ​Amaterasu her ‌own ​light, and ‌its ​dwelling at ‌Ise ​is her ​own
- ‌**Cave of ‌Heaven ‌(Ama-no-Iwato)** — ​The ​rock-door of ‌her withdrawal; ​in ​ritual memory ‌the ​sealed cave ​marks ‌every crisis ​in ‌which order ​must ​be coaxed ​back
- ​**Sun-disc** — ‌The radiant ‌disk ​she embodies, ‌echoed ​today in ​the ‌red circle ‌of ‌the Japanese ‌flag
- ​**Magatama beads** ‌— ​The curved ​jewels ​Izanagi gave ‌her; her ​own ​necklace generated ​the ‌gods of ​the ​ukei rite ​with ‌Susanoo
- **Shimenawa ​rope** ‌— The ​sacred ‌rope Ame-no-Futodama ​stretched ‌across the ‌cave mouth ​— ​the first ​boundary ​between retreat ‌and ‌the common ​world

mythology.body:
Amaterasu's mythology, told in the ​*Kojiki* and *Nihon Shoki*, is a theology of **light, ‌legitimacy, and the restoration of order** after violence. It ‌moves from her birth in purification to her withdrawal ​from a wounded heaven and her dispatch of the ​imperial line to earth.[^1]

### From the Left Eye of ​Izanagi (The Birth)

When Izanami died giving birth to ​the fire god and Izanagi failed to bring her ​back from Yomi, the grieving creator purified himself in ‌a river. As he washed his face, three sovereign ​deities were born: **Amaterasu** from his left eye, **Tsukuyomi** ​from his right eye, and **Susanoo** from his nose ‌(Kojiki 1). Delighted, Izanagi removed his own necklace of ​magatama and gave it to her, charging her with ‌rule of Takamagahara, the High Plain of Heaven. Her ​full style, Amaterasu-ōmikami — the Heaven-Illuminating Great August Deity — ‌is written with the very character for sky. The ​Nihon Shoki preserves several variant birth accounts, a reminder ​that these texts were compiled at court rather than ​received as fixed scripture. The myth makes the sun ​the eldest child of purification: light is what emerges ​once pollution has been washed away.[^2]

### Susanoo's Rampage in ‌Heaven (The Outrage)

Susanoo wept so violently at the ​death of his mother that mountains shook and rivers ‌swelled; when Izanagi expelled him from the land, the ​storm god climbed to heaven to bid his sister ‌farewell. Wary, Amaterasu went out armed, but Susanoo protested ​his innocence and proposed an *ukei*, a test by ‌which the siblings exchanged ornaments and produced divine children ​(Kojiki 1). No sooner was the pledge sealed than ‌he reversed the ridges of her rice-fields, filled the ​ditches, and flayed the heavenly piebald horse, hurling its ​carcass through the roof of her weaving hall. The ‌shock killed her weaving-maiden. Enraged and grieving, Amaterasu withdrew ‌into the rock cave and sealed the door. The ‌myth insists that the gravest danger to cosmic order ​is not foreign invasion but violence inside the family ​— the sun itself can be driven out by ‌her own brother.

### The Rock Cave of Heaven (The ​Withdrawal)

With Amaterasu hidden, the world went dark and ​the eight hundred myriad deities gathered on the bed ‌of the tranquil heavenly river to devise a remedy. ​The goddess **Ame-no-Uzume** overturned a tub, stamped upon it, ​and danced so bawdily that the assembled gods roared ‌with laughter (Kojiki 1). Curious, Amaterasu opened the rock-door a ​crack: why did they rejoice in darkness? Uzume answered ‌that they had found a deity more splendid than ​her — and held up the **yata mirror**. As ​the sun leaned out to look, the strong-handed **Ame-no-Tajikarao**, ​concealed behind the door, seized her wrist and drew ​her into the light; Ame-no-Futodama stretched the first *shimenawa* ‌across the cave mouth so she could never withdraw ‌again. The myth is a charter for communal restoration: ​light returns not through force but through laughter, cunning, ‌and a mirror that lets the goddess see her ​own radiance.

### Ninigi and the Three Regalia (The Descent)

​To bring order to the unruly land below, Amaterasu ‌resolved to send her grandson **Ninigi-no-mikoto** to rule the ‌earth (Nihon Shoki 2). The embassy had not been ‌easy: her first envoy lingered in heaven, the second ‌was charmed by the earthly god Ōkuninushi, and a ​third chose marriage over mission. At last she entrusted ‌Ninigi with the **Three Sacred Regalia** — the curved ​magatama jewel, the yata mirror, and the sword Kusanagi ​— instructing him to revere the mirror as if ​it were herself. Ninigi descended to Mount Takachiho, wed ‌Konohanasakuya-hime, and from their line sprang **Jimmu**, first emperor ​of Japan. The myth is transparently political — a ​charter in which the ruling house descends from the ​sun — yet its mechanism is veneration: heaven does ‌not rule the earth directly; it sends a sign ​the earth must honor.

### The Mirror Goes to Ise ​(The Journey)

Though born in heaven, Amaterasu did not ​remain in the palace. The Nihon Shoki (reign of Suinin) ‌tells how the goddess longed for the land of ​Yamato, 'the land of fair rice-ears of the fertile ‌reed-plain,' and commanded that a sanctuary be built for ​her there. In the Kojiki's account she had first ‌taken up residence inside the imperial palace itself, troubling ​the emperor's house, until she declared her wish to ‌leave. The emperor's daughter, the princess **Yamato-hime**, wandered the ‌provinces carrying the divine mirror, divining for a dwelling-place, ​until she received the oracle on the banks of ​the Isuzu river. There rose the **Ise Grand Shrine**, ​where the mirror is enshrined to this day and ​the sanctuary is renewed every twenty years. The myth ‌moves the sun out of the palace and into ‌a perpetual sanctuary: sovereignty becomes devotion, and devotion requires ​a building that never ages.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki 1–2 (variant births, Yamato-hime and the founding of Ise).

syncretism.body:
In ​the medieval ‌*honji-suijaku* ‌system Amaterasu ​was identified ​with ​the cosmic ​Buddha ​Vairocana (Dainichi ‌Nyorai) ​— the ​sun ‌of the ​Dharma itself ‌— ​and Buddhist ‌chapels ​and sutras ​stood ​within Ise's ​precincts ​until the ‌Meiji separation ​edicts. ‌State Shinto ​then ‌stripped away ​these ‌Buddhist layers, ​taught ‌the descent ​of Ninigi ​as ‌national history, ‌and ‌made her ​the ​theological center ‌of ​imperial ideology; ​overseas shrines ‌carried ​her cult ​into ‌the empire. ​Her ‌modern reception ​extends ​to the ​video game ​*Ōkami*, ‌whose wolf-goddess ‌is ​drawn from ‌her ​iconography — ​evidence ‌that the ‌sun still ‌needs ‌a face.[^1]

​Kindred ‌figures in ​the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ​index ‌include [[ise|Ise]] ​(shrine and ​enshrined ​sun goddess), ‌[[izanagi|Izanagi]] ​(father and ​sun ​goddess), [[ninigi|Ninigi]] ‌(solar ​grandmother and ‌divine grandson), ​[[ra|Rꜥ]] ‌(sun / ​light), ‌[[susanoo|Susanō]] (storm-sun ‌sibling ​rivalry), and ​[[tajikarao|Tajikarao]] ​(strong hand ​opens the ‌cave ‌of the ​sun).

archaeology.body: The ​Ise ‌Grand ‌Shrine ​(Mie ​Prefecture) is ​Amaterasu's ​principal ​dwelling: ‌its ​Inner ​Shrine ‌(Kōtai ​Jingū), ‌traditionally ​founded in ‌the ​reign ​of ​Suinin ​(1st ​century ‌BCE), ​is ‌rebuilt every ​twenty ‌years ​(shikinen-zōtai) ‌on ​alternating ‌adjacent ​plots, ​a ‌rite ‌documented from ‌690 ​CE ​and ‌continued ​without ​break. ‌Architectural ​and ​documentary ‌study of ​the ‌precincts ​— ​the ​Uji ​Bridge, ‌the ‌Shōden, ​the ‌treasure halls ​— ​makes ‌Ise ‌the ‌best-documented ‌ritual ​complex ‌in ​Japan, ​though the ​mirror ‌itself ​is ​never ​displayed. ‌Heian ​ritual ​compendia ​(Engishiki) and ‌shrine ​records ‌(Shintōshū) ​list ‌the ​annual ‌offerings ‌of ​cloth ​and first ​fruits ​presented ‌by ‌the ​court.[^1]

meditation.body:
Amaterasu ​teaches that ‌light ‌is not ​automatic. ​Her withdrawal ​shows ​that even ​the ‌sun can ​be ​wounded ‌into silence, ​and ‌her return ​shows ‌what it ​takes ​to heal ​her: ​not argument, ​not ‌force, but ​the ‌laughter of ​Uzume ‌and the ​honesty ‌of a ​mirror. ‌The community ​of ​gods succeeds ‌precisely ‌because ‌each plays ​a ​part — ‌the ​dancer, the ​strong-arm, ‌the ritualist, ​the ​mirror-bearer.

To ‌read ​the myth ‌politically ​is correct ​but ​incomplete: it ​is ‌also a ‌psychology ​of withdrawal ‌and ​return. ​Everyone who ‌has ‌sealed themselves ‌behind ‌a rock ​door ‌knows that ​the ​way back ​is ‌not a ​plea ​but a ​celebration ‌worth peeking ​at. ​And the ​mirror ‌matters most ​of ‌all: she ​returns ‌not ​because others ‌praise ‌her, but ​because ​she is ​allowed ​to see ‌her ‌own radiance ​reflected.[^1]
